notes.title: Autonomy is the dial; reliability, cost and latency are the meters

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
You call it a dial. Isn't autonomy qualitative — a kind of design, not a quantity?
Tier 2 — Trade-off

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The complexity ladder this note puts numbers on — Anthropic: building effective agents

  • What consistency costs a headline number, measured — τ-bench (arXiv 2406.12045)

  • The provable-security version of the same trade — Defeating prompt injections by design — CaMeL (arXiv 2503.18813)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • the architects framing — the complexity ladder and the over-building failure mode.

  • the 95% problem — multiplicative compounding.

What this note adds: the correction to the framing. It isn't a three-way trade between equals — autonomy is the one variable you set, and reliability, cost and latency are all monotone functions of it. Saying that, with the numbers, is the staff-round move.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why it isn't a triangle? One dial, three meters. All three move with step count.
Reliability at 20 steps, 97% each? 0.54. At 50 steps, 0.22.
Cost of doubling autonomy? ~3.4× tokens — the growth term is quadratic.
The only lever that improves all three? Cutting steps. Everything else trades.
What to say out loud? Where you're landing on the ladder, and what you gave up.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The framing everyone uses is a triangle — autonomy against reliability against cost and latency — and it's slightly wrong in a way that matters. Autonomy is expressed as steps the model chooses, and every one of the other three is a function of step count: reliability falls multiplicatively, cost grows quadratically because context is re-billed, latency grows linearly. So it's one dial and three meters, not a three-way trade. What that buys you in a round is a defensible answer to "why not more autonomous": at 97% per step, twenty steps is 54% and fifty steps is 22%, and I'd rather ship a workflow that works than an agent that impresses.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Lowest rung that fits Default. The task decomposes into known steps. Capability on the inputs you didn't anticipate. The steps are the same every time.
Bounded autonomy Path varies, but a step cap and gates hold. The production default. Design effort on caps, gates and recovery. Step count varies but the work is recognisable.
High autonomy Genuinely open-ended, and failure is cheap. Reliability and cost, both superlinearly. Research, exploration, no side effects.
Autonomy as the goal Never. All three meters, for a property nobody asked for. "We want it to be fully agentic."

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Lowest rung A workflow graph; the model at named nodes. Cheapest, most predictable p95. Failures name a function; on-call is ordinary.
Bounded autonomy A loop with caps, gates and a degradation path. Cost varies with the step distribution's tail. You monitor step count as a leading indicator.
High autonomy Few constraints, heavy observability, hard budgets. Long tail dominates the bill — O(N²) on p99 runs. The pager fires for quality, not availability.

The redraw test: moving down a rung removes boxes and adds determinism, which is why it's the rare architectural change that improves every number at once. That's the same property §8 gives "fewer steps" and §10 gives "cut steps" — three sections reaching the same lever from different directions is usually a sign it's the real one.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Reliability is exponential in the dial. With per-step success s over N steps, task success is sᴺ. At s = 0.97:

N = 5   → 0.86
N = 20  → 0.54
N = 50  → 0.22

Nothing in that table is a prompt problem. A step success rate of 97% is already good; the loss is the exponent.

Cost is quadratic in the same dial. From §10, total input is N·c₀ + g·N(N−1)/2. At c₀ = 4,000, g = 1,500: ten steps is 107,500 tokens and twenty is 365,000. Doubling autonomy costs 3.4× the money and roughly halves the success rate — one decision, both consequences.

Latency is linear, which makes it the mildest of the three. Σ over steps, so doubling steps doubles wall-clock. It's the meter people watch because it's the visible one, and it's the one that punishes autonomy least.

What the literature shows about the top of the ladder. τ-bench reports state-of-the-art agents under 50% at pass@1 and under 25% at pass^8 on rule-bound tasks — the reliability meter at real autonomy, measured. And CaMeL's 77% against 84% undefended shows the same shape on the security axis: constraining what the agent may do costs seven points of capability. Both are arguments for landing low and justifying each rung up.

The asymmetry worth stating. Every lever except one trades: routing trades quality for cost, caching trades layout discipline for both, gates trade latency for reliability. Cutting steps improves reliability, cost and latency together, because it moves the dial the other three depend on. That's why "can this be a workflow" is the highest-value question in any agent design round.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The third question is the one that makes this an architect's diagram rather than a preference: it asks you to compute sᴺ against a stated product bar before choosing. A candidate who does that arithmetic unprompted has answered "why not more autonomous" before it was asked.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The demo did the whole task end to end. In production it finished about half the time."

Root cause. The demo was a curated happy path of six steps; real inputs needed eighteen to twenty-five because the agent had to handle ambiguity the demo input didn't contain. Per-step behaviour was unchanged and good — the same 97%-ish reliability throughout — but 0.97⁶ is 83% and 0.97²² is 51%. The team read the drop as a model problem and spent a quarter on prompt work and a model upgrade, which moved per-step reliability from roughly 97% to 98% and end-to-end from 51% to 64%: real, and not the fix.

Fix. Nine of the steps were re-derivable from data the system already had, so they moved into deterministic code, taking the trajectory to about twelve steps — and 0.98¹² is 78%, on the model they already had. The late cost was the quarter spent on the wrong lever — and the reason it was spent is that nobody had written sᴺ on a whiteboard, which would have shown in ten minutes that per-step improvements can't reach the target from twenty-two steps.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You call it a dial. Isn't autonomy qualitative — a kind of design, not a quantity?

It's qualitative in how it's described and quantitative in what it costs. The rungs are discrete — single call, workflow, agent, multi-agent — but what actually drives the meters is the number of model-chosen steps each rung produces, and that's a number you can estimate before building anything.

That's what makes it usable in a round. "More autonomous" is unfalsifiable; "this rung means about twenty steps, which at our per-step rate is 54%" is a claim someone can push back on. Converting the qualitative ladder into the step count it implies is most of the value of the framing.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

If autonomy is that expensive, why build agents at all?

Because the alternative isn't a cheaper agent, it's a system that can't handle the input. A workflow handles exactly the paths you enumerated, and for tasks where the path genuinely depends on what you find — debugging, research, investigation — enumerating them isn't possible, so the comparison isn't 54% against 90%, it's 54% against nothing.

The discipline is to pay for autonomy only where that's true. Most real systems are mostly enumerable with a few genuinely open decisions, which is why the strong answer is usually a workflow with agentic nodes rather than a choice between the two. You're buying autonomy by the step, and you should be able to say which steps you bought.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What happens to this picture at 100× traffic?

The exponent doesn't change — it's a per-run property — but the variance becomes the story. Cost is O(N²) so the p99 step count dominates the bill: if p50 is 8 steps and p99 is 40, each p99 run costs about 25 times a p50 run and 1% of traffic can be a quarter of spend. Reliability distributes the same way, so your worst runs are both the most expensive and the most likely to fail.

That makes the step cap a capacity control as much as a reliability one, and it's an argument for reporting the step distribution rather than the mean. A mean step count hides exactly the tail that pays for everything.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

A product manager wants the agent to handle 100% of cases autonomously. What do you say?

I'd convert it into the arithmetic and hand it back as a choice. At our per-step reliability, full autonomy over this task implies roughly this many steps, which implies this success rate and this cost per run — and then ask which of those they'd like to change, because the three move together.

Usually the answer lands on a split: autonomous on the 70% of cases that are recognisable, escalating on the rest. That's a better product than 100% autonomy at 54%, and it's a better business case, because the escalation path is cheap and a wrong autonomous answer is not.

The part worth volunteering is that 100% autonomy is rarely the actual goal — the goal is usually cost per resolved case or time to resolution, and autonomy was a proposed means. Re-deriving the requirement from the metric is the architect move, and it frequently reveals that the cheapest path to the real goal involves less autonomy rather than more.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "It's a trade-off triangle — you pick two of autonomy, reliability and cost."

✅ Reality: It's one dial and three meters. Reliability, cost and latency are all functions of step count, so they move together. Nothing lets you hold two while raising autonomy.

❌ Trap: "We'll get end-to-end reliability up with a better model."

✅ Reality: 97% → 98% per step over 22 steps takes you from 51% to 64%. Real, and not enough. Past a point the exponent beats the base, and the lever is the exponent.

❌ Trap: "Latency is the cost of autonomy."

✅ Reality: Latency is the mildest of the three — linear in steps. Reliability is exponential and cost is quadratic. Watching the visible meter while the other two move faster is the common mistake.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • the architects framing — the ladder this note quantifies.

  • the 95% problem — the compounding behind the reliability meter.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §1 Which rung of the ladder does this task need — this is the arithmetic behind that choice.

  • §8 Buy reliability with fewer steps or with verification gates — the same lever, from reliability.

  • §10 Which factor of the steps² term you attack — the cost meter.

  • §15 Which axis is growing — run length is one of the three, and this is why it hurts most.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 "Our agent succeeds 60% and costs too much" — this arithmetic is the first thing that brief needs.

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — the design where landing low is the whole answer.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Reading traces before proposing fixes — Anthropic: demystifying evals for AI agents

  • Two planning failures that look like model failures — ReAct: synergizing reasoning and acting (arXiv 2210.03629)

  • The span contract that makes classification possible at all — OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Planning failure modes — derailing and premature termination.

  • Failure modes & resilience — the failure taxonomy at the call layer.

What this note adds: the discriminator. §14's triage says "classify the failures" and the four buckets are named in the index; what decides an architect round is knowing what evidence assigns a trace to a bucket — because each one has a different fix and the default answer is always "model".

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The four buckets? Planning · tool · context · model.
The discriminator? What you'd have to change to fix it.
The default misdiagnosis? Everything filed as "model" — so the fix is a prompt or an upgrade.
Which bucket is invisible without raw tool results? Tool — the agent narrates a failure as success.
What the classification produces? A ranked list, not a rate.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I classify before I fix, and the discriminator I use is "what would I have to change to make this trace succeed". If the right information was present and the agent chose the wrong next step, that's planning. If the call was right and the result was wrong or unusable, that's tool. If the answer was in the window three steps ago and isn't now, that's context. Only if the information was present, the call was right, the context was intact and it still got it wrong is it the model — which is the smallest bucket and the one everything gets filed under by default, because it's the one you can fix by rewriting a prompt.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Planning failure The info was there; the next step was wrong. Control-flow work: a graph, a plan, or fewer choices. Derailing, wandering, stopping early.
Tool failure The call was right; the result wasn't usable. Schema, validation and error-contract work. Errors narrated as success; unparseable results.
Context failure It knew, then didn't. Retrieval or budget work — what gets cut and when. Facts from early steps contradicted later.
Model failure Everything else was intact. A prompt, an upgrade, or accepting the ceiling. Genuinely hard reasoning, correct inputs.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Planning An explicit graph, or a plan-then-execute split. Fewer wasted steps; often cheaper. Re-plan rate becomes the metric to watch.
Tool Stricter schemas, validation at the boundary, real error contracts. Negligible. Tool error rate separates from agent error rate.
Context Retrieval as a tool, or a different eviction order. Compaction or retrieval calls. Context hit rate; what got cut and when.
Model Nothing structural. An upgrade, or routing up. You've accepted a ceiling — say so explicitly.

The reason this classification is worth doing before any fix is that three of the four rows change the architecture and one doesn't. A team that files everything under "model" spends its quarter on the only row with no structural lever, which is exactly the quarter the failure story below describes.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The classification is cheap and it is the whole deliverable. Forty failed traces, hand-read, sorted into four buckets: an afternoon. What comes out is a distribution rather than a rate, and the distribution is what tells you where the quarter goes. A 60% success rate is unactionable; "of 40 failures, 22 are context, 11 tool, 5 planning, 2 model" is a plan.

Why forty. You're estimating proportions to decide priority, not to publish. At n = 40, the standard error on a proportion near 0.5 is √(0.25/40) ≈ 0.079 — about eight points, which is easily enough to tell a 55% bucket from a 12% one. Chasing tighter than that spends days to refine a ranking you already have.

The discriminator, stated as a procedure. For each failed trace, in order:

  1. Was the needed information in the model's input at that step? No → context.
  2. Did a tool return an error, or a result the agent couldn't use? Yes → tool.
  3. Given correct input and a usable result, was the chosen next step wrong? Yes → planning.
  4. Otherwise → model.

The order matters because it puts the cheapest-to-check and most-commonly-true conditions first, and it puts "model" last by construction — which is the correction this note exists to make.

Why the tool bucket is systematically undercounted. A tool error the agent narrates as success looks, in a trace that stores the model's summary, like a clean successful step. You cannot separate bucket two from bucket four without raw tool arguments and raw results on the span — which is why the span contract from §12 is a prerequisite for this classification rather than a nice-to-have.

What each bucket costs to fix, roughly. Tool is cheapest — schemas and error contracts are ordinary engineering. Context is next — a retrieval change or a different eviction order. Planning is structural: a graph or a plan/execute split. Model is either an upgrade or an admission. That ordering rarely matches the distribution, which is the point: you fix by impact, not by ease.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

"Model failure" is the only terminal node with no question after it, and it's drawn in the alarm colour deliberately — reaching it means you've accepted a ceiling rather than found a lever. A classification where most traces land there is usually a classification done without raw tool results.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We spent a quarter on prompt engineering and the success rate moved three points."

Root cause. Failures had never been classified. The working assumption — reasonable, and untested — was that a 61% success rate meant the model was getting things wrong, so the team iterated on instructions and eventually upgraded the model. When someone finally read forty traces, more than half were context failures: a summarisation step was dropping order identifiers from the history, so by step nine the agent was reasoning correctly about an order it could no longer name. No prompt could fix that, because the instruction was being followed and the fact was gone.

Fix. Identifiers were pinned into a structured slot that compaction couldn't touch, which is a change to the eviction order rather than to any prompt, and success moved eleven points in a week. The expensive part was the quarter, and the reason it was spent is that the trace viewer rendered the agent's summaries beautifully and nobody had asked what the retrieval step had actually returned.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Aren't these overlapping? A context failure causes a planning failure.

They cascade, and the classification is about the first thing that went wrong, not the visible symptom. A dropped identifier at step four produces a wrong tool call at step nine, and the wrong call is what you notice — but filing it under planning sends you to fix control flow, which was working correctly on bad inputs.

That's why the discriminator walks the trace forward and asks where the first defect appears, rather than examining the final error. It's the same discipline as root-cause analysis anywhere else, and the reason agents make it hard is that the compounding is invisible in a rendered transcript that reads fluently at every step.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Forty traces by hand doesn't scale. Why not classify with a judge?

Eventually, yes — and not first. The first classification is also where you learn what the buckets mean for your system, and that understanding is what lets you write a rubric a judge could apply. Automating before you've done it once produces a judge that confidently applies categories nobody has grounded.

Once the hand-classification exists it doubles as the calibration set: run the judge against your forty labelled traces, measure agreement, and only then use it on the next four hundred. That ordering also protects you from the ceiling — a judge agreeing with you 80% of the time is fine for ranking buckets and not fine for a precise proportion.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Does the distribution stay stable as the system changes?

No, and that's the useful part. Fixing the top bucket redistributes the rest, so the classification is a repeated measurement rather than a one-off diagnosis — and each round it points somewhere different. A team that classifies once and works the list for two quarters is working a stale list.

At scale the composition shifts predictably: tool failures fall as schemas harden, context failures rise with trajectory length, and planning failures rise with autonomy. So the distribution is also a readout on which of those three you've been increasing, which makes it a useful thing to put next to the step-count distribution.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Build me the tooling that makes this routine rather than heroic.

Three pieces, and the first is not tooling. Spans must carry raw tool arguments and raw results, or bucket two is invisible and everything lands in bucket four — so the span contract comes before the classifier. Second, a sampled stream of failed runs into a review queue with the four buckets as one-click labels, because the cost of classification is almost entirely context-switching. Third, the labels write back onto the trace, so the distribution is a query rather than a spreadsheet someone maintains.

Once labels exist, the judge can be calibrated against them and run continuously, with the human queue sampling to check agreement. That gives a live distribution per release, which is the thing you actually want — a bucket that jumps after a deploy names the regression before anyone bisects.

The part I'd raise unprompted is that this is the same pipeline as the online-eval loop in §12. Failed runs, labelled by humans, feeding a distribution and an eval set is one system, and building it twice — once for debugging and once for evaluation — is the usual waste.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Success is 60%, so the model isn't good enough."

✅ Reality: That's a conclusion drawn before any classification. Model failure is usually the smallest bucket and the only one with no structural fix — it's the default answer because it's the one you can act on without reading traces.

❌ Trap: "The trace shows the agent handled the tool result fine."

✅ Reality: The trace shows the agent's summary of the result, unless spans carry raw tool output. That's precisely the case where an error was narrated as success, and it's the whole tool bucket.

❌ Trap: "We fixed the top bucket, so now we work the second one."

✅ Reality: Fixing the top bucket redistributes the rest. Re-classify after each fix; the list you generated a quarter ago is describing a system that no longer exists.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Planning failure modes — the planning bucket's contents.

  • Failure modes & resilience — the call-layer taxonomy.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §12 What a span must carry — raw tool results are a prerequisite for this classification.

  • §12 Which production signal you're willing to treat as a label — the same review queue.

  • §5 What gets cut when the window fills — where the context bucket gets fixed.

  • §3 An explicit graph, or a free loop — where the planning bucket gets fixed.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 "Our agent succeeds 60% and costs too much" — this note is step three of that triage.

  • §14 Coding agent — tests localise failures, so the buckets are unusually easy to assign.

If it's all existing patterns, what makes agent reliability hard at all?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
When does leading with the backend framing actually hurt you?
Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling
Which of these patterns stops mapping cleanly at scale?
Tier 4 — Open-ended design
A platform team asks what they need to build for agents. What's the list?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Compensating transactions, which is what a failed agent run needs — microservices.io: saga

  • Atomically recording an intent and the effect that follows it — microservices.io: transactional outbox

  • The agentic vocabulary these map onto — Anthropic: building effective agents

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • reliability engineering — the reliability patterns as they appear in agents.

  • Failure modes & resilience — timeouts, retries, fallback, breakers at the call layer.

What this note adds: the framing decision, and the mapping table it rests on. Both vocabularies describe the same machinery; which one you open with changes how the room reads you, and the cost of getting it wrong runs in both directions.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The claim in one line? A failed agent run is a distributed transaction. Same patterns.
What leading with backend framing buys? Credibility, and a shorter route to the hard parts.
What it risks? Sounding like you're avoiding the AI-specific question.
The one genuinely new thing? The step that fails is chosen by a model, so you can't enumerate paths.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Almost everything in agent reliability is a backend pattern with a new label: a partially-completed run is a saga needing compensation, record-before-effect is the outbox, safe retries need idempotency keys, a failing provider needs a circuit breaker, and an overloaded queue needs backpressure. With a staff interviewer from a distributed-systems background I lead with that, because it moves us past the vocabulary to the hard parts in about a minute. With an AI-native interviewer I lead agentic and reach for the mapping when the reliability question arrives — because opening with "this is just microservices" reads as deflection to someone whose question is about the model. What I never do is claim there's nothing new: the genuinely new part is that a model chooses which step runs, so the path can't be enumerated in advance.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Lead backend The interviewer's background is distributed systems. Reads as deflection if their question was about the model. They probe consistency, failure and state before prompts.
Lead agentic AI-native room, or the question is about model behaviour. You may spend minutes re-deriving patterns they know. They open on autonomy, tools, evals.
Map explicitly, both ways Mixed panel. The safest default. Two sentences of overhead per pattern. A panel with a platform engineer and an ML engineer.
Claim nothing is new Never. The non-determinism, which is the actual hard part. "It's just a workflow engine with an LLM in it."

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Backend framing None — it's the same system, named differently. None. Your existing on-call and runbooks mostly transfer.
Agentic framing None. None. You'll rebuild patterns your platform team already runs.
Explicit mapping None, and reuse becomes visible. Cheaper — the outbox you already have is the one you need. The platform team can own half of it.

The reason this is a real decision despite changing no boxes is that it changes who builds it. A team that frames durable agent execution as novel writes its own checkpointing; a team that recognises a saga reuses the workflow engine, the outbox and the idempotency keys already in production. The framing decides the build-versus-reuse conversation before anyone writes code.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The mapping, one to one. Each row is a pattern the room already knows and the agentic decision it becomes:

Backend pattern In an agent Decision note
Saga + compensation A run that failed after three effects landed §7 Partial completion
Transactional outbox Record the intent before the effect, not after §11 Audit trail
Idempotency keys What makes a retried tool call safe §8 What is safe to retry
Circuit breaker A failing provider or tool, failed fast §8 Fallback and breakers
Backpressure What the queue does when it can't keep up §7 Queues and backpressure
Durable workflow Checkpoint, resume, human pause §7 Checkpointing
Bulkhead / quota Per-tenant spend and rate isolation §10 Spend caps

Seven rows, seven existing implementations in most companies. That is the argument for the framing: it converts "build a durable agent runtime" into "route the agent through the workflow engine we already run".

What genuinely is new, and it's one thing. In a normal distributed transaction the sequence of steps is written in code, so the compensation path is enumerable and testable. In an agent the next step is chosen by a model at runtime, so the set of reachable effect sequences is not known in advance. Every consequence follows from that: compensations must be registered dynamically as effects land rather than written as a fixed reverse path; the reachability audit in §11 exists because you can't read the paths off the source; and the eval problem in §12 is hard because you can't enumerate what to test.

The two-sentence version, for the room. "Everything below the model is a distributed system and the patterns are the ones you'd expect — saga, outbox, idempotency, breakers, backpressure. The one thing that's genuinely different is that the step sequence is chosen at runtime, so the paths can't be enumerated, which is why the compensation registry and the gate audit are dynamic rather than static." That pair of sentences is the highest-leverage thing in this note.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The converging node is the point of the diagram: whichever way you opened, you have to arrive at what's actually new. Leading backend without it sounds dismissive of the problem; leading agentic without it sounds unaware that the problem is mostly solved.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We built a durable execution layer for the agent. Six months in, we found the platform team had one."

Root cause. The agent team framed the problem in agentic vocabulary — checkpointing, resumable runs, human-in-the-loop pauses — and the platform team's system was described in workflow vocabulary: durable execution, activities, signals, compensation. Both were solving the identical problem and neither recognised the other's, because the words didn't collide in any planning document. The agent team built checkpointing, a resume path, a pause primitive and an at-least-once effect story, all of which existed and were production-hardened one floor away.

Fix. The agent moved onto the existing workflow engine, with model calls as activities and tool effects as compensatable steps. The six months weren't entirely wasted — the dynamic compensation registry genuinely didn't exist, because the platform engine assumed a statically-known step sequence. That residue is the real lesson: the mapping is one to one on the patterns and not on the assumptions, so the framing saves you the seven rows above and leaves you the one thing that's new.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

If it's all existing patterns, what makes agent reliability hard at all?

That the step sequence is chosen at runtime by a model. A saga in a normal service has a fixed set of steps, so you write the compensating transaction for each one and test the reverse path. An agent may call tools in an order no one enumerated, so you can't write the reverse path in advance — you register a compensator as each effect lands and unwind whatever actually happened.

That single property is what makes the audit in §11 a graph-reachability problem rather than a checklist, and why eval needs trajectories rather than cases. The patterns transfer; the assumption that the path is known doesn't, and that assumption is baked into a lot of existing tooling.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

When does leading with the backend framing actually hurt you?

When the interviewer's question was about the model and you answered about infrastructure. If they ask how you'd stop the agent hallucinating a refund amount and you start on idempotency keys, you've answered a question they didn't ask and signalled that you reach for familiar ground. That reads as avoidance even when the infrastructure answer is also needed.

The tell is what they probe first. Consistency, state and failure questions invite the backend framing; autonomy, tools and eval questions want the agentic one first, with the backend mapping offered as reinforcement once the model-level answer has landed. Getting the order right is worth more than the content of either.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Which of these patterns stops mapping cleanly at scale?

Backpressure, because the scarce resource isn't yours. Classic backpressure protects your own capacity, and you control the consumer, the queue and the worker pool. With an agent the binding constraint is usually the provider's tokens-per-minute budget, which you can't scale by adding workers — more workers multiply concurrent calls into the same ceiling and make it worse.

Circuit breakers shift too. A breaker normally trips on errors, but the characteristic model failure is a 200 with a worse answer, so an error-rate breaker never fires. Tripping on a quality signal instead means the breaker's input is a sampled statistical measure rather than a per-call outcome, which changes its response time from seconds to minutes and its false-positive story completely.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

A platform team asks what they need to build for agents. What's the list?

Mostly a list of things they already have, which is the useful answer. Durable execution, an outbox, idempotency, breakers, quotas and per-tenant isolation are all in their existing stack; the work is exposing them to the agent runtime rather than building them. I'd start there explicitly, because it shortens the roadmap by quarters and puts the reliability story in the hands of the team that already operates it.

What's genuinely new is short: a compensation registry that accepts handlers at runtime rather than a statically-declared reverse path; a gate audit over the tool graph, since paths aren't readable from source; and a quality-based breaker, because error rate doesn't detect the failure that matters. Those three are the agent-specific build.

The part I'd raise unprompted is on-call. Everything above transfers; the pager does not, because an agent's characteristic incident is a quality regression with every health check green. That's the one place where the "no new physics" framing genuinely runs out, and pretending otherwise is how a team ends up with a runbook nobody can execute.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Agent reliability is a new field."

✅ Reality: Seven of the patterns you need are in your company already — saga, outbox, idempotency, breakers, backpressure, durable workflow, quotas. Recognising that is the difference between a quarter and a sprint.

❌ Trap: "It's just a workflow engine with an LLM in it."

✅ Reality: The path is chosen at runtime, so compensations can't be pre-written, gates can't be read off the source, and tests can't enumerate cases. That's one difference and it invalidates several assumptions.

❌ Trap: "Reuse the existing circuit breaker and you're covered."

✅ Reality: It trips on errors, and the failure you care about returns 200. A breaker for agents needs a quality signal, which makes it slower and statistical rather than per-call.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • reliability engineering — the patterns in agentic form.

  • Failure modes & resilience — the call-layer version.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §7 What happens to the effects a failed run already caused — the saga row, in full.

  • §8 What you fail over to, and what trips the breaker — the breaker row, including the quality signal.

  • §13 Where the seam goes — this framing is what makes reuse visible.

  • §15 Who owns the tool contract, the eval set and the pager — where the framing stops transferring.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Internal agent platform for many teams — the reuse argument is most of that design.

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — a workflow engine with LLM nodes, framed correctly.

📚 Reference Links

  • Per-scope budgets and keys, which is what ownership looks like in a gateway — LiteLLM proxy: budgets and rate limits

  • Tool schemas as a published contract rather than a local detail — MCP specification: authorization

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • the architects framing — the architect's posture these responsibilities implement.

What this note adds: the allocation, and the one responsibility that doesn't transfer. Tool contracts and eval sets have obvious owners once you ask who bears the blast radius — the pager is the hard one, because an agent's characteristic incident is a quality regression with every health check green.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Who owns a tool contract? Whoever owns the system it acts on — they bear the blast radius.
Who owns the eval set? The product team. It encodes what "correct" means for them.
Why the pager is hard? The incident is a quality drop with every health check green.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Two of these allocate themselves once you ask who carries the consequence. A tool contract belongs to the team owning the system behind it, because a loose schema there is their outage and their data. An eval set belongs to the product team, because it's a written definition of correct for their domain. The pager doesn't resolve cleanly: an agent's typical incident is a quality regression no availability alert detects, so whoever holds it needs a signal — escalation rate, canary task success — that most rotations don't have and can't act on at 3am. Naming that gap beats assigning the rotation.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Platform owns everything One or two agents, one team. Becomes the bottleneck and the blame sink for domains it doesn't know. A small org with a central AI team.
Product teams own everything Few shared tools, high autonomy culture. Every team reinvents tenancy, tracing and budgets — badly. Divergent quality and no shared eval.
Split by artifact Anything multi-team. The default. A registry and a review process to run. Tools shared across agents.
Nobody owns the pager The accidental default. Quality regressions live in production for days. The alert list has latency and errors, nothing else.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Platform owns all Central gateway, central everything. Efficient, until it's a queue. One team paged for every team's agent.
Products own all N implementations of the same substrate. Duplicated spend and effort. No comparable metrics across agents.
Split by artifact Registry owns schemas; product owns prompts and evals; platform owns gateway, tracing and budgets. Reuse where it's shared. Clear escalation path per artifact.

The allocation, stated. Tool contract — the owning system's team, since a wrong schema is their incident; the registry enforces that it's declared, versioned and effect-classified. Prompts and graph — product; they are the product. Eval set — product, because it defines correct for their domain, with the platform supplying the harness. Gateway, tracing, budgets, tenancy — platform. Model version — platform, with a notice period, because it's a global change.

Why the pager is genuinely different. Availability on-call works because failure is a signal: a 500, a timeout, a saturated queue. An agent failing produces 200s at normal latency with worse answers, so the paging signal is statistical — a shift in escalation rate or canary success, which needs a bake window and can't be diagnosed by restarting anything. So the runbook's first action is usually roll back the artifact version: no live intervention fixes a quality regression.

The practical split. Platform keeps the availability pager. Product holds a quality alert on a metric they chose — usually escalation rate — routed to business hours, because a quality regression is rarely more urgent overnight than a rollback in the morning. Forcing quality into a 3am page is the failure mode: it either never fires or fires on noise.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "A schema change shipped on Friday and the agent stopped resolving a third of its tickets. Nobody was paged."

Root cause. A downstream team tightened validation on an endpoint the agent's refund tool wrapped — a correct, announced change to their own API. The tool's schema lived in the agent team's repo and wasn't updated, so calls failed validation, the agent narrated them as inconclusive and escalated. Every dashboard was green: no errors, normal latency, slightly higher escalation. The announcement went to consumers of the API, and nobody had recorded that an agent tool was one.

Fix. Tool contracts moved into a registry owned by the team behind each system, so schema and change lived together and the agent became a declared consumer; a quality alert on escalation rate went to product in business hours. The late cost was three days of degraded resolution absorbed as support load — and the discovery that nobody could name who owned the refund tool, which is the question this note exists to make answerable beforehand.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • the architects framing — the posture these roles implement.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §4 Adopt MCP, and build a server or consume one — the registry is where contract ownership gets enforced.

  • §12 Which production signal you're willing to treat as a label — the quality alert's input.

  • §13 What the versioned unit is — rollback is the agent pager's first action.

  • §15 Lead with the backend framing, or with the agentic one — the pager is where that framing stops transferring.

📚 Reference Links

  • The provider ceilings that bind before your compute does — Anthropic: rate limits

  • What consistency does to a headline number as tasks lengthen — τ-bench (arXiv 2406.12045)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • deployment and scaling — the scaling shapes.

What this note adds: the disambiguation. "How does this change at 10×?" is three different questions with three different answers, and the strongest move is asking which axis before answering — because the one that breaks first is rarely the one they meant.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The three axes? Tools · tenants · run length.
Which is worst, and why? Run length — cost is quadratic, reliability exponential.
What 10× tools breaks first? Tool selection — the catalogue outgrows the prompt.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I ask which axis before answering, because they break completely different things. Ten times the tools breaks selection first — the catalogue no longer fits the prompt, so tools get retrieved per run and descriptions become an interface. Ten times the tenants breaks isolation and capacity — four surfaces need a tenant key, and one customer's batch job can drain the token budget for everyone. Ten times the run length is the brutal one, because cost is quadratic and reliability is exponential in steps, so it's the only axis where 10× of the input is far more than 10× of the pain. Most people mean traffic and say 10×; traffic is the easy one.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
10× tools Catalogue growth, many teams contributing. Retrieval in the hot path, and descriptions become an API. Selection accuracy falling as tools are added.
10× tenants Multi-tenant product growth. Isolation on four surfaces, and capacity allocation. One customer's spike degrading another's latency.
10× run length Task scope growing. The dangerous one. Cost grows ~100×, reliability collapses. Step-count p99 drifting up release over release.
10× traffic only Straightforward growth. Compute and provider ceilings. The axis people usually mean, and the mildest.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Tools A registry and per-run tool retrieval. Retrieval cost per run. Selection accuracy becomes a tracked metric.
Tenants Namespaced memory, traces, caches; per-tenant credentials and budgets. Reserved capacity sits partly idle. Per-tenant dashboards; noisy-neighbour triage.
Run length Fewer steps, or recovery; caching becomes mandatory. Quadratic — the p99 tail dominates the bill. Step distribution becomes a headline metric.
Traffic Queue-driven autoscaling on in-flight runs. Provider ITPM binds before compute. Capacity planned in tokens, not requests.

Why run length is the one to fear. From §10, total input is N·c₀ + g·N(N−1)/2, and from §15's dial note, task success is sᴺ. Take a run from 10 steps to 100: input tokens go from about 107,500 to roughly 7.8 million, a 73× increase for a 10× input — and at 97% per step, success falls from 74% to 5%. No other axis has that shape; tools and tenants scale roughly linearly with engineering effort.

Why traffic is the mild one. It's the axis everyone has scaled something along before. The agent-specific twist is only that the ceiling is provider tokens per minute rather than your own compute, and that caching raises effective throughput because cache reads don't count toward ITPM. Otherwise it's ordinary capacity work.

The move in the round. Answer "which axis?" first, then pick the one that breaks soonest for this design and say why. A research agent's risk is run length; a platform's is tenants; an enterprise assistant's is tools. Naming the binding axis before designing for it is the difference between a scaling answer and a list of scaling techniques.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We planned for 10× traffic. What killed us was the tenants."

Root cause. Capacity work had been done properly — workers scaled on in-flight runs, a provider limit increase was negotiated, caching was on. What nobody modelled was that 10× the customers meant 10× the distinct prompt prefixes, so the shared cache hit rate collapsed from around 80% to under 20%. Effective throughput fell with it, because cache reads that don't count toward the input-token limit had been quietly carrying a large share of capacity. The token budget was then exhausted at a fraction of the planned traffic, and the first symptom was interactive users getting 429s.

Fix. Prompt layout was restructured so the platform-static prefix came first and tenant-specific content second, restoring a shared cached segment across all tenants, with per-workspace reservations so no single tenant could drain the pool. The late lesson is the one this note exists for: the team had scaled the axis they anticipated, and the axis that actually moved interacted with a capacity assumption nobody had written down.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • deployment and scaling — the scaling mechanics.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §13 Which traffic gets the tokens when the provider says no — the capacity interaction in the failure story.

  • §15 Autonomy is the dial — why the run-length axis is the violent one.
